page.title: The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI - Jan van den Berg
page.description: An update to Brooks's Law in the age of AI.
page.text_excerpt: Jan van den Berg Home About Quotes Search 🇳🇱 RSS The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI 27 October 2026 Last weekend I watched four people desperately trying to get a laptop to connect to a screen. I was happily observing their efforts, with zero intent to join in. But someone nudged me: can't you have a look at it? My reply: "Haha sorry no! My experience is that adding more people will not solve this problem any quicker". I was of course -- indirectly -- referring to Brooks's Law: "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." It was formulated by computer scientist Frederick P. Brooks Jr. in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, based on his experience managing the IBM OS/360 project. However I got to thinking. Does this still hold up in the age of AI agents and LLMs? At first glance, you’d think no. The traditional bottlenecks -- onboarding time, endless stand-ups, and office politics -- disappear overnight. An AI agent is up to speed in milliseconds and doesn't demand a coffee break. But when you look closer, and the law hasn't vanished. It just mutated. The famous "Baby Problem" remains: nine agents still can’t deliver a baby in one month. Sequential tasks are still sequential. Overhead hasn't disappeared; it shifted: instead of managing people, you are now managing agents. Someone still needs to define "done", review the code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together. That someone is you. Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop. Maybe the 2026 update to Brooks’s Law should be: "Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster." page.text_excerpt: SKIP TO MAIN CONTENT The homepage SUBSCRIBE SIGN IN Tech Reviews Science Entertainment AI Policy Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads 6 AI NEWS POLICY Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes. by Terrence O'Brien Oct 24, 2026, 6:32 PM UTC 6 6 Comments (All New) Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies, as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania. The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions. The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment.

Photograph: Jane Tregelles/Alamy Heritage Which is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debate Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest is from 1430 Helena Horton Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google With their low ceilings, timber beams and roaring fires, many of England’s inns lay claim to being the oldest in the land and to have been visited by Vikings and Saxons. But an archaeologist who worked on behalf of Historic England says not one of the more than two dozen pubs that make this claim is being accurate. While many claim origins dating back 1,000 years, Dr James Wright, a buildings archaeologist, said it was difficult to verify whether any pubs were built and used as inns or ale houses and kept in continuous use prior to the 1400s. After painstaking investigation, including tree-ring dating on the wooden beams of pubs – a process known as dendrochronology – Wright named the George Inn, of Norton St Philip, Somerset, as the oldest pub in England. It has fabric dating from the late 14th century. View image in fullscreen Inside the George, set up in the 14th century by the monks of Hinton Priory. Photograph: PR He told the Guardian: “Not one of the claimants to be the oldest pub (and there are over two dozen of them) are even vaguely close to being so in reality.” I stand to defend vertical drinking.
